items.name: ii-V-I in major
items.bass_implications: Root motion by descending fifth twice. A stepwise alternative puts the third of ii in the bass so the bass walks 4-5-1.
items.voice_leading_notes: The seventh of ii falls a half step to the third of V; the third of V rises to the tonic and the seventh of V falls to the third of I. Holding those two guide-tone lines is what makes the progression sound inevitable.
items.expected_destination: Imaj7 or a tonic substitute such as vi7 or iii7.
items.explanation_template: ii-V-I in {key}: {slot0} prepares the dominant, {slot1} supplies the tritone, and {slot2} resolves it. Guide tones move by step throughout.

items.name: ii-V-i in minor
items.bass_implications: Same descending-fifth bass as the major form; the flat sixth degree in iiø7 is what marks the minor version.
items.voice_leading_notes: The dominant normally carries b9 or b13 so its alterations resolve inward to chord tones of the minor tonic. Avoid the natural 13 on the dominant here.
items.expected_destination: i7, imMaj7 or i6 depending on how tonic the arrival should sound.
items.explanation_template: Minor ii-V-i in {key}: {slot0} darkens the predominant with a flat fifth, {slot1} adds altered tension, and {slot2} resolves to the minor tonic.

items.name: I-vi-ii-V turnaround
items.bass_implications: Bass descends by third then moves in fifths. Substituting VI7 for vi7 makes the bass identical but adds an applied leading tone.
items.voice_leading_notes: Every adjacent pair shares two common tones, so a four-part setting can move almost entirely by step.
items.expected_destination: Back to the top of the form, normally I.
items.explanation_template: Standard turnaround in {key}: two tonic-region chords lead through the predominant to the dominant so the form can repeat.

items.name: iii-VI7-ii-V turnaround
items.bass_implications: Bass falls in fifths from the mediant.
items.voice_leading_notes: VI7 is an applied dominant of ii, so its third must rise into the root of ii. Altering VI7 with b9 or b13 strengthens the pull.
items.expected_destination: I or Imaj7 at the top of the next chorus.
items.explanation_template: Applied turnaround in {key}: the mediant substitutes for tonic and each chord becomes the dominant of the next.

items.name: Diatonic circle of fifths
items.bass_implications: Bass alternates falling fifths and rising fourths so it stays inside one octave.
items.voice_leading_notes: Sevenths chain: each chordal seventh becomes the third of the next chord and falls by step. Alternate complete and incomplete voicings to avoid parallel fifths.
items.explanation_template: Descending-fifth sequence through every diatonic degree of {key}; the chain of resolving sevenths is the mechanism, not the individual chords.

items.name: Descending fifths in minor
items.bass_implications: Continuous falling fifths; the flat sixth degree appears as a bass note twice.
items.voice_leading_notes: As in the major sequence, the sevenths chain downward by step. The raised seventh appears only in the final dominant.
items.explanation_template: Minor descending-fifth sequence in {key}, ending with the only functional dominant in the chain.

items.name: Lament bass
items.bass_implications: The defining feature is the chromatic descent 1 - 7 - b7 - 6 - b6 - 5 in the bass; the chords above it are whatever harmonises that line.
items.voice_leading_notes: Upper voices should stay as static as possible so the descending bass is the only thing that moves. Common tones do most of the work.
items.expected_destination: The dominant, or a Phrygian arrival on bII.
items.explanation_template: Lament bass in {key}: a stepwise chromatic descent from tonic to dominant in the bass, harmonised above.
items.notes: Encoded here by its bass line rather than by fixed roman numerals, because the harmonisation varies widely while the bass does not.

items.name: Minor line cliche
items.bass_implications: Static bass on the tonic throughout. The motion is entirely in an inner voice.
items.voice_leading_notes: One voice descends 1 - 7 - b7 - 6 while the others hold. Give that line to a single voice and do not let it jump registers.
items.explanation_template: Line cliche over a static {key} minor tonic: one inner voice descends chromatically while the chord root stays put.

items.name: Major line cliche
items.bass_implications: Static tonic bass.
items.voice_leading_notes: The descending line 1 - 7 - b7 - 6 sits in an upper or inner voice. When it reaches b7 the chord becomes an applied dominant of IV, which is usually where it goes.
items.explanation_template: Major line cliche in {key}: a descending chromatic voice turns the tonic into an applied dominant of the subdominant.

items.name: Twelve-bar blues
items.bass_implications: Roots only in the classic form; the bass may add the sixth and flat seventh as a boogie figure.
items.voice_leading_notes: Dominant sevenths do not resolve here. The seventh of I7 is a stable chord member, and parallel motion between I7 and IV7 is idiomatic rather than an error.
items.expected_destination: Back to bar one, or a tonic ending in place of the final V7.
items.explanation_template: Twelve-bar blues in {key}: all three primary chords are dominant sevenths and none of them carries a resolution obligation.
items.notes: The last bar is the turnaround; replace V7 with I7 for a closed ending.

items.name: Quick-change blues
items.bass_implications: Same root plan as the plain blues but with a ii-V in bars nine and ten.
items.voice_leading_notes: From bar seven onward the guide tones start behaving functionally again, so the chordal sevenths should resolve down by step through the turnaround.
items.explanation_template: Quick-change blues in {key}: the subdominant arrives a bar early and the last four bars are a functional turnaround.

items.name: Jazz blues
items.bass_implications: Bar four introduces an applied ii-V into IV; bar six uses a chromatic passing diminished chord that keeps the bass moving by half step.
items.voice_leading_notes: The passing diminished chord in bar six is linear: spell it ascending and resolve it into the first inversion of the tonic.
items.explanation_template: Jazz blues in {key}: the blues skeleton with applied dominants, a passing diminished chord and a full turnaround.

items.name: Minor blues
items.bass_implications: Roots throughout; the flat sixth in bar nine is the only chromatic bass note.
items.voice_leading_notes: Unlike the major blues, the dominant in bars ten and twelve is functional and its alterations should resolve into the minor tonic.
items.explanation_template: Minor blues in {key}: minor sevenths on i and iv, with a real altered dominant in the last four bars.

items.name: Backdoor cadence progression
items.bass_implications: Bass rises a whole step into the tonic instead of falling a fifth.
items.voice_leading_notes: The seventh of bVII7 lies a half step above the major third of the tonic and falls into it. That single voice is the whole mechanism.
items.explanation_template: Backdoor approach in {key}: a borrowed subdominant pair resolves upward by whole step, with the flat seventh degree falling into the major third of tonic.

items.name: Tritone-substitute ii-V
items.bass_implications: Bass descends chromatically 2 - b2 - 1, which is the main reason to make the substitution.
items.voice_leading_notes: bII7 shares its tritone with V7, so the guide tones barely move; the ninth of bII7 is the leading tone of the key.
items.explanation_template: Tritone substitution in {key}: the dominant is replaced by a dominant seventh a tritone away, converting the bass into a chromatic descent while keeping the same tritone resolution.

items.name: Dorian vamp
items.bass_implications: Two roots a fourth apart, repeated. Keep the tonic in the bass on the strong bar so the mode does not flip to the relative major.
items.voice_leading_notes: Hold common tones between the two chords and let only the natural sixth degree move. Any leading tone destroys the mode.
items.expected_destination: Itself: the vamp is a loop, not a progression toward a cadence.
items.explanation_template: Dorian vamp on {key}: the major subdominant exposes the natural sixth degree that distinguishes Dorian from Aeolian.

items.name: Mixolydian vamp
items.bass_implications: Root motion down a whole step and back.
items.voice_leading_notes: The two triads share no tones, so contrary motion between outer voices keeps the loop from lurching.
items.explanation_template: Mixolydian vamp on {key}: the flat seventh triad falls to the tonic without any leading tone.

items.name: Lydian vamp
items.bass_implications: Roots a whole step apart with the tonic returning on strong bars.
items.voice_leading_notes: The raised fourth degree is the common thread; place it in an upper voice so it is audible and never harmonise it with a plain IV triad.
items.explanation_template: Lydian vamp on {key}: the major supertonic triad keeps the raised fourth degree in play without implying a modulation.

items.name: Phrygian vamp
items.bass_implications: Bass alternates by half step, which is the entire identity of the mode.
items.voice_leading_notes: Keep the flat second in the bass or the top voice. Buried in an inner voice it just sounds like a wrong note.
items.explanation_template: Phrygian vamp on {key}: the half step above the tonic is the defining colour.

items.name: Diatonic planing
items.bass_implications: The bass moves in parallel with every other voice; it carries no independent line.
items.voice_leading_notes: All voices move in strict parallel motion. Parallel fifths and octaves are the texture, so those penalties must be suppressed for this schema.
items.expected_destination: Any chord; planing is a texture rather than a functional path.
items.explanation_template: Diatonic planing in {key}: a single voicing shape moved stepwise through the scale, so colour rather than function drives the passage.

items.name: Chromatic planing
items.bass_implications: Parallel bass with the rest of the texture.
items.voice_leading_notes: Constant structure: the identical voicing is transposed bodily. Do not correct the parallel perfect intervals; correcting them destroys the effect.
items.explanation_template: Chromatic planing from {key}: one voicing shape transposed without regard to key, producing constant-structure harmony.

items.name: Andalusian cadence progression
items.bass_implications: Stepwise descending bass 1 - b7 - b6 - 5.
items.voice_leading_notes: Upper voices should also descend so the whole texture falls; the arrival on V usually carries a major third, which turns the mode Phrygian dominant.
items.expected_destination: The Phrygian arrival on V is itself the goal; the figure then repeats.
items.explanation_template: Andalusian descent in {key}: a four-step stepwise fall from the minor tonic to a major dominant.

items.name: Doo-wop changes
items.bass_implications: Roots; the bass may descend 1 - 6 - 4 - 5 or invert IV to keep the line stepwise.
items.voice_leading_notes: Adjacent chords share two, one and one common tones respectively, so an upper-voice setting can be almost entirely stepwise.
items.explanation_template: Doo-wop loop in {key}: tonic, tonic substitute, predominant, dominant - a complete functional circuit designed to repeat.

items.name: Axis loop
items.bass_implications: Bass falls a third, then a fourth, then rises a fifth. Starting on vi makes the loop ambiguous between the major key and its relative minor.
items.voice_leading_notes: Every adjacent pair shares two common tones, which is why the loop tolerates almost any melody over it.
items.explanation_template: Axis loop in {key}: four chords with maximal common-tone connection and a deliberately ambiguous tonic.

items.name: Descending-third sequence
items.bass_implications: Bass descends by step through the scale for the first six chords, then rises to the dominant.
items.voice_leading_notes: The sequence works because every second chord is in root position while the pattern alternates falling fourths and rising seconds; suspensions on the strong beats are the usual decoration.
items.expected_destination: Cadence on V or back to I.
items.explanation_template: Descending sequence in {key}: alternating fifth and step root motion produces a stepwise descending bass.

items.name: Minor plagal loop
items.bass_implications: Bass moves up a fourth and back, or stays on a tonic pedal while the upper voices supply iv.
items.voice_leading_notes: The borrowed flat sixth degree falls by half step back to the fifth of the tonic. That half step is the entire effect, so keep it in an exposed voice.
items.explanation_template: Minor plagal motion in {key}: the borrowed minor subdominant colours the tonic without any dominant.

items.name: Chromatic mediant chain
items.bass_implications: Bass falls by major third each time, returning to the tonic after three moves.
items.voice_leading_notes: Each pair shares exactly one common tone; hold it and move the other voices by step or half step. Do not try to justify these chords functionally.
items.expected_destination: Tonic, by symmetry after three moves.
items.explanation_template: Chromatic mediant chain from {key}: major triads related by major third, connected by common tone rather than by function.

items.name: Two-chord drum-and-bass loop
items.bass_implications: Two roots only, each held for a full bar or longer. The bass part is rhythmically busy but harmonically static; harmonic rhythm and drum tempo are independent.
items.voice_leading_notes: Maximum common-tone retention so the pad never re-articulates. The ninth of the tonic chord is the third of the flat sixth chord, so one voice can hold throughout.
items.explanation_template: Two-chord loop in {key}: slow harmonic rhythm underneath fast rhythmic activity, held together by a retained common tone.
items.notes: Explicitly encoded to demonstrate that harmonic rhythm must not be inferred from tempo.

items.name: Neo-soul mediant descent
items.bass_implications: Bass steps down 1 - 3 - b3 - 2 with a chromatic passing root.
items.voice_leading_notes: The major seventh chord on the lowered third degree is a passing sonority between iii7 and ii7; keep the upper voices nearly static and let the bass carry the chromaticism.
items.expected_destination: V7, V7sus4 or straight back to the tonic.
items.explanation_template: Mediant descent in {key}: a chromatic passing chord smooths the step from the mediant to the supertonic.

items.name: Applied dominant chain
items.bass_implications: Each applied dominant sits a fifth above its target, so the bass alternates leaps and steps.
items.voice_leading_notes: Every applied chord introduces a raised tone that must rise and a seventh that must fall. Failing either resolution makes the tonicisation read as a wrong note.
items.explanation_template: Applied dominant chain in {key}: each target degree is briefly tonicised before the real dominant arrives.

items.name: Tonic pedal prolongation
items.bass_implications: The bass holds the tonic under all four chords; only the upper voices change.
items.voice_leading_notes: Chords above a pedal are judged on colour and smoothness rather than root motion. Dissonances against the pedal need no preparation as long as they move by step.
items.expected_destination: A real cadence once the pedal releases.
items.explanation_template: Tonic pedal in {key}: the bass never moves, so the upper harmony becomes decoration of a single sustained chord.

items.name: Ascending passing diminished
items.bass_implications: Chromatic ascent 1 - #1 - 2 in the bass. The diminished chord exists to fill that half step.
items.voice_leading_notes: Purely linear. Spell the diminished chord with a raised root ascending, not with a flat second, or the resolution will look like a descent.
items.explanation_template: Passing diminished chord in {key}: a chromatic connector between tonic and supertonic with no functional claim of its own.

items.name: Neapolitan approach
items.bass_implications: First inversion puts scale degree 4 in the bass, so the bass line is unchanged from an ordinary predominant.
items.voice_leading_notes: The flat second falls to the leading tone, an awkward diminished third. Either fill it in with a passing tone or hand the two notes to different voices.
items.explanation_template: Neapolitan approach in {key}: a major triad on the lowered second degree intensifies the predominant before the dominant.

items.name: Augmented sixth approach
items.bass_implications: Bass sits on the flat sixth degree and falls a half step to the dominant.
items.voice_leading_notes: The augmented sixth between b6 and #4 expands outward to an octave on scale degree 5. Routing the German form through a cadential six-four avoids the parallel fifths a direct resolution would create.
items.explanation_template: Augmented sixth approach in {key}: two voices expand outward by half step onto the dominant from opposite directions.

items.name: Suspended pedal vamp
items.bass_implications: One static bass note for both chords.
items.voice_leading_notes: The fourth resolves to the third when the suspension releases, but in modal and neo-soul profiles it can simply alternate without ever resolving.
items.expected_destination: Tonic, or nothing at all if the vamp is the whole section.
items.explanation_template: Suspended vamp on the dominant of {key}: the fourth alternates with the third over an unchanging bass.

items.name: Stepwise ascending bass
items.bass_implications: Bass ascends 1 - 2 - 3 - 4 by step; the inverted chords exist to support that line.
items.voice_leading_notes: The passing chord is in first inversion so the bass stays stepwise; its tritone resolves inward into the tonic sixth chord.
items.expected_destination: The predominant and then a cadence.
items.explanation_template: Stepwise ascent in {key}: inversions chosen so the bass walks up the scale rather than leaping between roots.

items.name: Power-chord riff loop
items.bass_implications: Roots doubled at the octave; the bass is the riff.
items.voice_leading_notes: Voiced as bare fifths, so successive chords are parallel fifths by construction. The parallel-perfect penalty must be disabled for this schema.
items.explanation_template: Power-chord loop in {key}: modally neutral fifths moved in parallel, with the riff rather than voice leading carrying the music.
